title: Where law comes from
summary: Law is a stack of layers: constitution, statutes, regulations, by-laws, the cases that interpret them, and the private law you write in your own contracts. Common-law and civil-law systems put the weight in different places. Knowing which layer answers your question is the first legal skill a developer needs.
body:
Law is a stack, not a single book. The constitution sits on top, then statutes, then regulations and by-laws, then the court decisions that interpret all of them, and your own contracts write private law for the people who signed. Before you pay anyone to answer a legal question, know which layer the answer lives in.

Recall

Q. What is the development spread?

A. Yield on cost minus the market capitalisation rate for the finished, stabilised asset. It is the margin you are paid for taking development risk, and if it is thin, the risk is not being paid for.

Q. How do you back into an implied land price from public information?

A. Estimate the completed value, subtract every cost and the profit a developer would require, and what is left is what the land can carry. That residual is the most a rational buyer would pay.

Q. Why can a profitable project run out of cash?

A. Because profit records revenue and expense when they are earned or incurred, while cash moves on its own timetable: draws, deposits, retainage and lender holdbacks. Profit on paper does not pay a contractor on Friday.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, every asset you will ever own is a bundle of legal rights. Title is a right. A building permit is a right granted under a statute. A loan is a set of promises with remedies attached. A construction contract is private law that you and a contractor wrote together. The value of each one depends on whether it can be enforced, by whom, and how fast. A developer who cannot tell a statute from a by-law, or a binding court decision from a persuasive one, pays lawyers to explain the basics and still cannot judge the advice he gets. This week is not about turning you into a lawyer. It is about knowing the shape of the system well enough to ask the right question and to recognise a weak answer.

The stack

Plain English first. Picture a building with floors. The top floor is the constitution: it says who is allowed to make law and what limits they must respect. Below it are statutes, the laws passed by an elected legislature. Below those are regulations, the detailed rules a minister or agency writes because a statute gave it the power to do so. Below those, in most places, are municipal by-laws, such as zoning rules, made under powers a higher legislature delegated to the city. Running through every floor are the decisions of courts, which tell you what the words actually mean when people disagree. And alongside the whole building sits contract: the private rules that only bind the people who agreed to them.

The professional framing is hierarchy and authority. A lower layer must stay inside the power the higher layer gave it. A regulation that goes beyond what its parent statute allows can be struck down. A by-law that conflicts with a valid provincial or national law usually gives way. And a contract cannot sign you out of a rule the law says is mandatory, such as many safety, consumer protection or tax rules. When you read a document, ask two questions: under what authority was this made, and is there anything higher up that overrides it?

Worked example one, with hypothetical round numbers. A city zoning by-law requires 1.0 parking space per apartment. A hypothetical regional statute, passed later, caps parking requirements at 0.5 spaces per unit within walking distance of a transit station. Your hypothetical 100-unit site sits near a station. Under the by-law you build 100 spaces; under the statute you may build 50. At a hypothetical 40,000 dollars per structured space, the difference is 50 times 40,000, which is 2,000,000 dollars of cost. Which layer governs is not an academic point; it is two million dollars. Whether the statute actually overrides the by-law in a real case depends on its wording and on how courts have read it, so verify that against the primary source before you rely on it, and get the answer in writing from local counsel.

Say that out loud now.

Two families: common law and civil law

Most of the world's legal systems belong to one of two families. In a common-law system, which came out of England, much of the law was built up by judges deciding cases one at a time, and statutes are layered on top of that judge-made foundation. Most of Canada, the United States, England, and Guyana work this way, with local variations. In a civil-law system, which came out of continental Europe, the core of private law is written down in a comprehensive code, and judges reason from the code. Quebec, France, much of Latin America and much of continental Europe and East Asia work this way.

Professionally, the difference changes how you read and draft. In a common-law system, the statute alone does not tell you the answer; you need the cases that interpret it. Contracts tend to be long because the parties spell out what happens in each situation rather than relying on default rules. In a civil-law system, the code supplies many default terms, scholarly commentary carries real weight, and contracts can be shorter. Professionals in civil-law systems, such as notaries in Quebec, often play roles in property transactions that a common-law lawyer would not.

Worked example two. A hypothetical partner from a civil-law country sends a six-page joint venture agreement. Your common-law counsel returns it as a sixty-page draft. Neither is careless. The six pages lean on a code that fills the gaps; the sixty pages exist because, without the clauses, a common-law court has fewer default rules to fill them. The real question is which system's gap-fillers apply to your deal. That is decided by the governing law clause, which you will meet again tomorrow.

Precedent: why one judge's words bind another

Precedent means that a court follows the legal reasoning of earlier decisions. In a common-law system, a lower court is bound by the decisions of the higher courts above it in the same hierarchy. Decisions from other courts, other provinces or other countries are only persuasive: a judge may find them helpful but need not follow them. And not every sentence in a judgment binds. The reasoning that was necessary to decide the case is what binds; remarks made in passing do not.

A famous example shows how one case can travel. In Donoghue v Stevenson, decided by the House of Lords in 1932, a woman said she became ill after drinking ginger beer from an opaque bottle that contained a decomposed snail. The court held that a manufacturer owed a duty of care to the person who would end up consuming its product, even without a contract between them. That reasoning was persuasive far beyond Scotland and England, and courts across the Commonwealth built their own negligence law on it. You will use it again in two weeks, when we study liability.

How the best do it

Large developers and contractors that work in many countries tend to keep what amounts to a jurisdiction sheet for each place they operate: the legal family, the court or arbitration route, how long enforcement realistically takes, which local firm advises them, and the governing law of their standard documents. A small developer can copy that in one page per jurisdiction and keep it current. It turns a vague feeling about a country into specific questions for counsel.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming the rules you know apply where you are going, whether across a border or across a provincial line. The control is a written answer from a lawyer licensed in that place, before you commit money, to three questions: which law governs this deal, which court or tribunal decides a dispute, and how long it realistically takes to enforce a judgment. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer licensed in the jurisdiction.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads a statute, finds the sentence that helps him, and stops. In a common-law system, the cases that interpret the statute may say something quite different. The opposite mistake is just as common: finding one helpful case and treating it as the law, without checking whether a higher court has since said otherwise, or whether it came from a court whose decisions do not bind yours.

Callback

In week 2 you learned the outside view: before trusting your own forecast, look at how similar projects actually turned out. Legal questions deserve the same discipline. When counsel says you have a strong case, ask for the reference class: in disputes like this one, before courts like this one, how often does the party in your position win, and how long does it take? A lawyer who answers with specifics is worth more than one who answers with confidence.

Recap

Law is a stack: constitution, statutes, regulations and by-laws, the court decisions that interpret them, and your own contracts. Lower layers must stay within the power given by higher ones. Common-law systems lean on judge-made precedent; civil-law systems lean on a code. Binding precedent comes from courts above you in the same hierarchy; everything else is persuasive. Next: Ford, Failure Forensics, on a joint venture that never said which court would decide its disputes.
checklist: Name the layer: constitution, statute, regulation, by-law, case law or contract
Ask under what authority any rule or document was made
Check whether a higher layer overrides the rule you are relying on
Identify the legal family of every jurisdiction you work in
Read the cases that interpret a statute, not only the statute
Treat decisions from other courts and countries as persuasive only
Get written answers from local counsel on governing law, forum and enforcement time
Keep a one-page jurisdiction sheet for each place you operate
head: Field checklist
speak: Law is a stack. At the top is the constitution, which says who may make law. Below it are statutes passed by the legislature, then regulations written under powers those statutes delegate, then municipal by-laws like zoning. Courts interpret every layer, and contracts write private law for the people who sign them. A lower layer has to stay inside the power the higher layer gave it, so the first question about any rule is: under what authority was this made, and does anything higher override it? There are two main legal families. Common-law systems, like most of Canada and Guyana, build law through judges' decisions, so you must read the cases, not just the statute. Civil-law systems, like Quebec, rely on a written code. Precedent from a higher court in your hierarchy binds; everything else only persuades. terms: Statute — a law passed by an elected legislature, such as a parliament or provincial assembly.
Regulation — detailed rules made by a minister or agency under power delegated by a statute, and valid only within that power.
Precedent — the principle that courts follow the legal reasoning of earlier decisions, binding when it comes from a higher court in the same hierarchy and persuasive otherwise.

hostile.q: Your planning consultant says the new regional rule cuts your parking requirement in half. Why should I underwrite the lower cost before a single court has looked at it?
hostile.a: You should not, on the consultant's word alone. I have asked local counsel for a written opinion on whether the regional statute validly overrides the municipal by-law for this site. Until that opinion arrives, the base case carries the higher by-law figure, and the saving sits in a separate upside case. If the opinion confirms the override, we move it into the base case and I will show you the wording and any decisions that interpret it.

role: Failure forensics (with Cole, audit and integrity)
title: The contract that named no court
summary: A composite case: a cross-border joint venture signed a detailed agreement that never said which country's law governed it or where disputes would be decided. When the partners fell out, they fought for two years about where to fight before they fought about the money. The prevention rule is simple and it costs one paragraph.
body:
The most expensive dispute is the one where you spend the first two years arguing about which court gets to hear it. This is a composite example, built from patterns common in cross-border property ventures, and it shows how a missing paragraph can destroy a profitable project.

Recall

Q. What separates the cost approach to valuation from the income approach?

A. The cost approach asks what it would cost to rebuild the asset new, less depreciation, plus land. The income approach capitalises or discounts the income the asset produces. They answer different questions, which is why they can disagree.

Q. When you reverse engineer a competitor's deal from public data, what is the weakest input?

A. Usually the cost side, because land prices and rents are often visible while hard and soft costs rarely are. Every implied return inherits the uncertainty of the cost estimate.

Q. What does net present value tell you?

A. The value today of future cash flows, discounted at your required rate of return, minus what you invest. A positive figure means the project beats your required return; a negative one means it does not.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will partner with people in other provinces and other countries: landowners, investors, contractors. Every one of those relationships rests on a contract, and every contract is only as strong as the court that will enforce it. If the document does not say which law governs and where disputes go, the parties will fight about that first, and the cost of that fight is pure waste. Cole joins me today because this is a record-keeping and integrity failure as much as a legal one.

Step 1: Timeline

This is a composite example. A developer based in one country formed a joint venture with a landowner based in another to build a hypothetical 80-unit apartment building on the landowner's site. Month 0: a letter of intent. Month 4: a joint venture agreement of about forty pages, covering contributions, a profit split, a budget and a management committee. It contained no governing law clause and no dispute resolution clause. Month 18: construction began. Month 30: costs ran over, the landowner refused a capital call, and the developer stopped funding. Month 32: the developer sued in its home country. Month 33: the landowner sued in the country where the land sat. Months 33 to 57: both sides argued about which court had jurisdiction. The site sat half-built.

Step 2: Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. First, the parties used a template the developer had used at home, without adapting it for a cross-border deal. Second, they chose a single lawyer to paper the deal to save fees, and that lawyer was licensed in only one of the two countries. Third, when the dispute started, each side raced to file in the court it believed would favour it, rather than first trying negotiation or mediation.

Step 3: Assumptions

The developer assumed its home courts would hear any dispute, because that was where its office was. The landowner assumed the courts where the land sat would decide, because the asset was there. Both assumptions were reasonable and they could not both be right. Each side also assumed that a judgment from its chosen court could be enforced against assets in the other country. Whether a foreign judgment can be enforced depends on the rules of the country where you try to enforce it, and those rules vary.

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: Incentives

Cole's point: follow the incentives. The single lawyer was paid to finish a document quickly, not to stress-test it. The developer wanted to start construction before costs rose, so it accepted gaps. Once the dispute began, each party had an incentive to delay in the other's court and accelerate in its own. Litigation counsel on both sides were paid by the hour, so nobody in the room was paid to end the jurisdiction fight early. None of that is dishonest. It is simply how the structure was set up, and structure beats good intentions.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The landowner's own adviser flagged the missing dispute clause in a marginal note at month 3. The note was never answered. The template's definitions referred to a statute in the developer's home country that did not exist in the other country, which should have shown that the document was not built for this deal. The management committee had two members, one from each side, with no tie-breaker, so any serious disagreement had nowhere to go except court.

Step 6: Point of no return

The point of no return was month 4, the signing. Before signature, adding a governing law clause, a forum clause and an escalation ladder would have cost a few hours of drafting. After signature, both parties had to agree to amend, and once the project was in trouble, neither had a reason to agree to anything that weakened its position. The race to file at months 32 and 33 locked the failure in.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause was not the cost overrun. Overruns happen, and a well-drafted agreement gives them a path: notice, negotiation, mediation, then a named tribunal applying a named law. The root cause was a contract that assumed a single legal world when the deal lived in two. The overrun was the trigger; the missing paragraph was the cause.

The money, with hypothetical numbers

Worked example one. Suppose each side spends a hypothetical 300,000 dollars a year on lawyers during a two-year jurisdiction fight. That is 300,000 times 2 years times 2 parties, or 1,200,000 dollars, before anyone argues about who owes what. Add carrying costs: if the half-built project carries a hypothetical 20,000,000 dollars of debt at 8 percent interest, that is 1,600,000 dollars a year, or 3,200,000 dollars over two years. Total waste: about 4,400,000 dollars. A governing law clause would have cost perhaps a few thousand dollars in drafting time.

Worked example two. The value of the half-built structure also decays. If weather exposure and lost contractor knowledge add a hypothetical 5 percent to a remaining hard cost of 10,000,000 dollars, that is another 500,000 dollars, and a partially built building is hard to finance, sell or insure.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is signing a cross-border or cross-provincial agreement drafted from one side's template by a lawyer licensed on only one side. The control is to have counsel in each relevant jurisdiction review the dispute, governing law and enforcement clauses before signature, and to record in your decision journal who confirmed that a judgment or arbitration award could be enforced against the other party's assets. Professional sign-off required: lawyers licensed in each jurisdiction involved.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner skips the boilerplate. Governing law, jurisdiction, notices and dispute resolution sit at the back of the document under a heading called general provisions, and people stop reading by then. Those clauses do nothing on a good day and decide everything on a bad one.

Callback

In week 2 you learned the pre-mortem: imagine the project has failed and ask why. Run a pre-mortem on every partnership agreement. Assume the partners are not speaking in month 30. Now read the document and ask: where does this fight happen, under which law, and how long until it ends? If the document cannot answer, you have found your next drafting task.

Recap

A composite joint venture lost years and millions because its agreement did not name a governing law or a forum. Every contract that crosses a border needs a governing law clause, a forum or arbitration clause, an escalation ladder, and advice from counsel on both sides about enforcement. Rule 19: no cross-border agreement is signed until it names its governing law, its forum and its escalation ladder, and counsel in each jurisdiction has confirmed that the outcome can be enforced. Next: Priya, The Money, on what lenders pay for legal certainty.
rule: Rule 19: No cross-border agreement is signed until it names its governing law, its forum and its escalation ladder, and counsel in each jurisdiction has confirmed the outcome can be enforced.
checklist: Every agreement names its governing law
Every agreement names its court or arbitration forum
An escalation ladder runs from notice to negotiation to mediation to final decision
Counsel licensed in each jurisdiction has reviewed the dispute clauses
Someone has confirmed how a judgment or award would be enforced against the other party's assets
Templates are adapted to the deal, with foreign statute references removed
Any two-person committee has a tie-breaker or deadlock route
Unanswered adviser comments are closed out before signature
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite case. A developer and a foreign landowner signed a forty-page joint venture agreement with no governing law clause and no dispute clause. When costs ran over and the partners fell out, each sued in its own country, and they spent two years arguing about which court should hear the case. Each side spent hundreds of thousands a year on lawyers while the half-built project carried millions in interest. The overrun was only the trigger. The root cause was a contract written as if the deal lived in one legal world when it lived in two. The template came from one side, one lawyer drafted it, and an adviser's warning in the margin was never answered. Rule 19: no cross-border agreement is signed until it names its governing law, its forum and its escalation ladder, and counsel in each jurisdiction has confirmed the outcome can be enforced.
terms: Governing law clause — the contract term that states which jurisdiction's law will be used to interpret the agreement.
Forum clause — the contract term that states which court, or which arbitration body, will decide disputes.
Enforcement — the legal process of turning a judgment or arbitration award into actual payment or action, often against assets in another country.

hostile.q: Your joint venture partner is in another country. If he stops funding, how exactly do I, as your lender, see this resolved?
hostile.a: The agreement names the governing law and an arbitration forum, and it sets out a ladder: written notice, thirty days of negotiation between principals, mediation, then arbitration. Counsel in both countries have confirmed in writing how an award would be enforced against his interest in the venture and his other assets. There is also a dilution remedy, so his share falls if he misses a capital call, and you would not need to wait for the arbitration to finish before the project keeps moving.

title: What a lender pays for legal certainty
summary: Lenders price the legal system as well as the deal: how secure their claim is, and how long it takes to enforce it. Slow or uncertain enforcement shows up as lower leverage, higher rates, more conditions and legal opinions. That cost lands on your equity, and on your personal balance sheet.
body:
A lender is buying a promise plus a remedy. If the remedy is slow or uncertain, the lender charges for it in leverage, interest and conditions, and that charge comes straight out of your equity return.

Recall

Q. What does yield on cost measure?

A. Stabilised net operating income divided by total project cost. It tells you what the money you spent will earn once the building is full and running.

Q. If public data shows rents and a sale price, how do you test whether a competitor's land price made sense?

A. Build the residual: completed value less all costs less a required profit. If the price paid is above the residual, the buyer was either betting on growth, accepting a lower return, or knew something you do not.

Q. Why is a dollar received in three years worth less than a dollar today?

A. Because the dollar today can be invested and earn a return for those three years, and because the future dollar carries risk. Discounting converts future cash to today's value.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, two buildings can produce identical net operating income and still raise very different loans. The difference is often the law around them: how good the lender's security is, how cleanly title is recorded, and how long a lender waits to recover its money if you default. Understanding that lets you predict lender terms before you ask, choose jurisdictions and structures that borrow well, and recognise when a term sheet is pricing the legal system rather than your project.

What the lender is really buying

In plain English, a loan has two parts. The first is your promise to pay. The second is the lender's security: the rights it gets over your assets if you do not pay. Security on a property loan usually means a registered mortgage or charge over the land, plus assignments of key contracts, rents and insurance proceeds. The lender's question is not only whether you will pay, but if you do not, how much it will recover and how fast.

The professional framing is loss given default. A lender estimates the chance you default and the loss it would suffer if you did. That loss depends on the value of the security, the costs of enforcing it, and the time enforcement takes, during which interest stops arriving, taxes and insurance still have to be paid, and the property may lose value. Each of those depends on the legal system. A jurisdiction with clear title registration and a predictable enforcement process lowers the loss. A slow court process, uncertain priority among creditors, or weak registration raises it.

To manage this, lenders ask for a legal opinion: a formal letter from a lawyer confirming that the borrower exists, has authority to borrow, and that the loan and security documents are valid and enforceable in that jurisdiction, usually subject to stated assumptions and exceptions. The opinion costs money and takes time, and in some jurisdictions the lender will insist on counsel in two places.

Worked example one: time to enforce, in dollars

All numbers are hypothetical. A lender advances 10,000,000 dollars against a property worth 15,000,000 dollars. The borrower defaults. Compare two legal environments.

Environment A: enforcement and sale take 6 months. Unpaid interest at 8 percent for half a year is 400,000 dollars. Legal and sale costs are 300,000 dollars. Taxes and insurance during the period are 100,000 dollars. The property sells for 15,000,000 dollars less a 5 percent discount for a forced sale, which is 14,250,000 dollars. The claim is 10,000,000 plus 400,000 plus 300,000 plus 100,000, which is 10,800,000 dollars. The sale covers it with room to spare.

Environment B: enforcement takes 36 months. Unpaid interest is 8 percent times 3 years times 10,000,000, which is 2,400,000 dollars. Legal and sale costs are 700,000 dollars. Taxes and insurance are 600,000 dollars. The property, neglected for three years, sells at a 20 percent discount: 12,000,000 dollars. The claim is now 10,000,000 plus 2,400,000 plus 700,000 plus 600,000, which is 13,700,000 dollars. The lender is short 1,700,000 dollars. Same building, same borrower, a loss instead of a full recovery, purely because of time.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example two: who pays for that risk

A lender in environment B protects itself by lending less. Suppose your hypothetical project costs 20,000,000 dollars. In environment A, a lender offers 70 percent of cost: 14,000,000 dollars of debt and 6,000,000 dollars of equity. In environment B, the same lender offers 60 percent: 12,000,000 dollars of debt and 8,000,000 dollars of equity. If the project produces a profit of 3,000,000 dollars before the extra interest in environment A is considered, the simple return on equity is 3,000,000 divided by 6,000,000, which is 50 percent, against 3,000,000 divided by 8,000,000, which is 37.5 percent. This is a simplification, because lower debt also means lower interest. But the direction is the point: weaker legal certainty forces more equity into the deal, and equity is your most expensive and scarcest money.

Lenders may also respond with a higher interest rate, more reserves, cash management controls, or a demand that some documents be governed by the law of a jurisdiction they trust more. Those are market practice, not legal requirements, and they vary from lender to lender.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for your personal balance sheet. An asset is only worth what you can turn into cash, through a sale or a loan, within your time horizon. Property in a jurisdiction where enforcement is slow and title is uncertain borrows less and sells more slowly, so it is less liquid than its appraised value suggests. Apply a mental haircut when you list it, and do not count it toward your liquidity floor. The same logic applies in reverse to money owed to you: a loan to a partner or a vendor take-back mortgage is worth less if collecting it would take years in a slow court.

One more practical point for the pro forma. The lender's legal costs are usually charged to you, the borrower, and they belong in soft costs and finance costs as named lines, not inside a vague contingency. Ask early for fee estimates from the lender's counsel and from your own, in every jurisdiction involved. A cross-border loan with counsel in two places can carry noticeably higher closing costs than a domestic one, and a late surprise there comes straight out of your equity.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is underwriting your equity requirement using leverage figures from a different legal environment. The control is to get indicative terms from at least two lenders active in the actual jurisdiction before you commit to land, and to ask each one directly which legal factors drove their leverage and rate. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer licensed in the jurisdiction, for the enforceability opinion.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats the lender's legal requirements, the opinion, the title review, the registration of security, as overhead to negotiate down. They are the lender's measure of how safe your project is. Delivering them early and cleanly is one of the cheapest ways to improve your terms.

Callback

Two lessons ago, LEX taught the legal stack: statutes, regulations and the cases that interpret them. A lender's legal opinion is that stack applied to one loan. When a lender's counsel asks for a search of registered charges or confirmation of signing authority, they are checking the layers. And in week 11 you learned net present value: enforcement delay is simply a time value problem, with the recovery pushed years into the future and discounted.

Recap

A lender buys your promise and a remedy. The slower and less certain the remedy, the larger the expected loss, and the lender prices that through lower leverage, higher rates and more conditions. In the worked example, the same building produced a full recovery with six months of enforcement and a 1,700,000 dollar shortfall with three years. Weak legal certainty forces more of your equity into the deal. Next: REGA, The Rules, on reading a statute and comparing how Canada and Guyana build their legal systems.
checklist: Ask lenders which legal factors drove their leverage and rate
Get indicative terms from lenders active in the actual jurisdiction
Estimate enforcement time and cost as numbers, not impressions
Confirm title registration and priority of security early
Budget time and fees for the lender's legal opinion
Model the equity requirement at the leverage the jurisdiction supports
Apply a liquidity haircut to assets in slow-enforcement jurisdictions
Discount money owed to you by the time it would take to collect
head: Field checklist
speak: A lender is buying two things: your promise to pay and a remedy if you do not. The remedy depends on the legal system: how clear title is, how secure the mortgage is, and how long enforcement takes. Time is the killer. In my example, a lender with a ten million dollar loan on a fifteen million dollar building recovers in full if enforcement takes six months. If it takes three years, unpaid interest, costs and a neglected building turn the same loan into a one point seven million dollar loss. Lenders know this, so in slow jurisdictions they lend less, charge more and demand more conditions. That pushes more of your equity into the deal and lowers your return. On my own balance sheet, I treat assets in slow-enforcement places as less liquid than their appraisal suggests, and I value money owed to me by how long it would take to collect.
terms: Security — the rights a lender takes over a borrower's assets, such as a registered mortgage on land, that it can use to recover its money on default.
Loss given default — the share of a loan a lender expects to lose if the borrower defaults, after recovering what it can from the security.
Legal opinion — a formal letter from a lawyer confirming that a borrower, its authority and the loan documents are valid and enforceable in a stated jurisdiction, subject to listed assumptions.

hostile.q: You are asking for 70 percent of cost in a jurisdiction where our enforcement experience has been slow. Why should we not cap you at 55?
hostile.a: Because the security package addresses the time problem directly. Title is registered and searched, the mortgage is first-ranking, rents and insurance are assigned, and local counsel's opinion confirms enforceability. I have also offered an interest reserve covering eighteen months, which covers a long enforcement period without relying on the asset. If you still need a lower ratio, I would rather discuss a smaller loan with a lower rate than a lower ratio at the same rate.

title: Reading a statute, and two legal systems
summary: Statutes are read in a set order: definitions, purpose, the operative rule, exceptions and transitional provisions, then the regulations and cases that sit beneath them. Courts read words in context, not in isolation. Canada and Guyana share a common-law foundation but build and run their systems differently.
body:
Most expensive statutory mistakes come from reading one section in isolation. Read a statute in order: definitions, purpose, the rule, the exceptions, the transitional provisions, then the regulations and the cases. And always confirm which version is actually in force.

Recall

Q. In the checkpoint on the language of money, what is the difference between as-is and as-complete value?

A. As-is value is what the property is worth today in its current state. As-complete value is what it would be worth once the planned project is finished. Lenders lend against one or the other, and confusing them overstates what you can borrow.

Q. When you reverse engineer an implied rent from a competitor's pricing, what must you adjust for?

A. Incentives, free rent, unit size and finish level. Headline rent without those adjustments overstates what the market actually pays.

Q. On the three financial statements, where does a loan repayment appear?

A. In the cash flow statement as a financing outflow, and as a reduction of liabilities on the balance sheet. The principal repayment is not an expense on the income statement; the interest is.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, statutes and regulations set your permit conditions, your development charges, your tax exposure, your safety duties and the rules for selling units. You will read many of them yourself before you ever call a lawyer, and you should. A developer who reads legislation well asks sharper questions, spots risks early and spends less on advice. A developer who reads it badly builds a pro forma on a sentence that a definition two pages earlier quietly changed.

The reading order

Plain English: legislation is written as a system, so you read it as one. Start with the definitions section. A word like dwelling unit, building or owner may mean something narrower or wider than ordinary speech. Then read any purpose clause, which tells you what the legislature was trying to achieve. Then the operative provision, the rule itself. Then the exceptions and exemptions. Then the transitional provisions, which say how the law applies to things already under way when it changed. Then the regulations made under the statute, which often contain the numbers. Then the cases.

The professional framing is the modern approach to interpretation that many common-law courts use: words are read in their entire context, in their grammatical and ordinary sense, in harmony with the scheme of the statute, its object and the intention of the legislature. In Canada, the Supreme Court adopted that approach in Rizzo and Rizzo Shoes, decided in 1998. In practice it means a court will not let you win by pulling one sentence out of its setting.

Worked example one, hypothetical. A local development charge applies to each new residential unit, at a hypothetical 20,000 dollars per unit. You plan a 120-key apart-hotel and assume it is commercial, so no charge applies. The definitions section defines residential unit as any room or suite with sleeping and cooking facilities intended for occupancy, regardless of the length of stay. Your suites have kitchenettes. If that definition captures them, the charge is 120 times 20,000, which is 2,400,000 dollars. Whether it does depends on the full wording and how it has been applied, so verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Say that out loud now.

Which version is in force

Statutes change. Amendments are passed, some sections come into force on a date set later by the government, and regulations are replaced. The text you found online may be an unofficial consolidation that is out of date, or it may include amendments that are not yet in force. Professionals check three things: the version in force on the relevant date, the official source rather than a summary, and the transitional provisions.

Worked example two, hypothetical. A new energy performance rule takes effect on a stated date and applies to building permit applications filed after it. The transitional provision says complete applications filed before that date proceed under the old rule. Your application is filed one week before the date but missing one required drawing. If complete is defined to require every listed document, you may be under the new rule. Suppose compliance adds a hypothetical 2 percent to a 15,000,000 dollar hard cost: 300,000 dollars, for one missing drawing. The lesson is to read the transitional provision and the definition of complete before you plan your filing date.

One more distinction. Not everything an authority publishes is law. Guidelines, policy manuals, practice notes and website summaries may show how officials intend to use their discretion, and in practice they can matter a great deal to your approval. But they generally do not carry the force of a statute or regulation, and they can be changed without the process a law change requires. When a document drives a number in your pro forma, ask counsel two questions: is this binding, and on whom? A guideline that binds nobody is a forecast of behaviour, and you should treat it as one.

Two Systems: Canada and Guyana

This is a conceptual comparison only. Verify against primary source before relying on any point.

Canada is a federation. Its constitution divides law-making power between the federal Parliament and the provinces, and matters of property and civil rights fall largely to the provinces, which in turn delegate much land-use control to municipalities. That is why development rules, title systems and many approvals differ from one province to the next. Nine provinces and the territories use the common law for private law; Quebec uses a civil law system built on its Civil Code, where notaries play a central role in property transactions. The Supreme Court of Canada is the final court of appeal.

Guyana is a unitary state with a written constitution and a single National Assembly, so there is no provincial layer between the national legislature and local authorities. Its private law rests on a common-law foundation received from England, with a Roman-Dutch heritage from the Dutch colonial period that still shows in parts of property law and land transfer practice, including a court-supervised process for transferring land and a deeds registry that operates alongside a separate land registration system. Its courts include the High Court and the Court of Appeal, and Guyana accepts the Caribbean Court of Justice as its final court of appeal. Because the systems share common-law roots, Canadian and English decisions can be persuasive in Guyana, but they do not bind its courts.

The practical point: in Canada, ask which province and which municipality before you ask what the rule is. In Guyana, ask which land system the title sits in and what the transfer process requires before you plan your closing.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is relying on an out-of-date or unofficial text, or one section read without its definitions. The control is a short statute note in your file for every rule your pro forma depends on: the official source, the version date, the definitions you relied on, the transitional provisions, and counsel's confirmation. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer licensed in the jurisdiction.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner searches for a keyword, lands in the middle of a statute and reads the sentence that appears. He never sees the definition that narrows it, the exception that removes his case from it, or the regulation that supplies the number.

Callback

In week 13 you built sources and uses and learned that estimate classes carry different confidence. Treat statutory costs the same way. A development charge confirmed by counsel against the current regulation is a firm number; one read from a summary on a website is a placeholder, and your contingency should say so.

Recap

Read legislation in order: definitions, purpose, operative rule, exceptions, transitional provisions, regulations and cases. Courts read words in context. Confirm the version in force. Canada divides power between federal and provincial governments and runs both common and civil law; Guyana is unitary, common-law based with Roman-Dutch influences in property, and its final court is the Caribbean Court of Justice. Next: Roman, The Numbers, on whether to settle or fight.
checklist: Read the definitions section before the operative rule
Read the purpose clause, exceptions and transitional provisions
Find the regulations that supply the numbers
Confirm the version in force on the relevant date from an official source
Read the cases that interpret the provision
Write a statute note for every rule your pro forma depends on
In Canada, confirm the province and municipality first
In Guyana, confirm which land system holds the title and what transfer requires
head: Field checklist
speak: Read a statute in order. Start with the definitions, because words like residential unit or owner may not mean what you think. Then the purpose, then the rule, then the exceptions, then the transitional provisions that say how the law treats things already under way. Then the regulations, which usually hold the numbers, and the cases that interpret it all. Courts read words in context, so one sentence pulled out of its setting will not save you. Always confirm the version in force from an official source. Canada is a federation: provinces control much of property law and delegate land use to municipalities, and Quebec uses civil law. Guyana is a unitary state with common-law roots, Roman-Dutch influences in land transfer, and the Caribbean Court of Justice as its final court. In both places, I write a short statute note for every rule my numbers depend on, and I verify it against the primary source.
terms: Definitions section — the part of a statute that gives specific meanings to words used in it, which control how the rest is read.
Transitional provision — a clause that says how a new or amended law applies to matters already under way when it changed.
Coming into force — the date on which a statute or a section of it actually takes legal effect, which may be later than the date it was passed.

hostile.q: Your pro forma has no development charge on the apart-hotel suites. What is that based on?
hostile.a: On the definition of residential unit in the current by-law and the way the municipality has applied it to similar projects. I have a statute note in the file with the official text, the version date and counsel's written view. Because the suites have kitchenettes, counsel flagged a risk, so the charge sits in my downside case at full value and I am seeking written confirmation from the municipality before we close on the land.

title: Settle or fight: the expected value of a dispute
summary: A dispute is an investment decision: you spend money and time now for an uncertain outcome later. Expected value, discounted for time and adjusted for hidden costs, turns a gut feeling into a number you can compare with a settlement offer. The breakeven probability tells you how sure you need to be before fighting makes sense.
body:
Every lawsuit is an investment with a cost today and an uncertain payoff years from now. Price it like one: probability times outcome, minus costs, discounted for time, then compare it with the settlement on the table.

Recall

Q. What are the layers of the legal stack?

A. Constitution, statutes, regulations and by-laws, the court decisions that interpret them, and contracts as private law between the parties. Lower layers must stay within the power the higher ones gave them.

Q. When you reverse engineer a deal, why test the implied return against a reference class?

A. Because an implied return that is far from what similar deals earn usually means one of your inputs is wrong, not that the buyer is a genius or a fool.

Q. What discount rate turns a project's net present value to zero?

A. The internal rate of return. It is the single rate at which the discounted inflows exactly equal the discounted outflows.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a developer is always in some dispute: a contractor's claim, a neighbour's complaint, a buyer who walked, a consultant who missed a deadline. Most are settled, and the ones that are not often should have been. Lawyers can tell you how strong your case is. Only you can decide whether fighting is worth the money, the time and the attention it takes away from the project. That decision is arithmetic, and it is yours.

The method in plain English

Draw the decision as a tree. One branch is settle: you pay or receive a known amount now. The other branch is fight: you pay legal costs over time, and at the end you either win or lose, each with an outcome and a probability. Multiply each outcome by its probability, add them up, subtract the costs, adjust for time, and you have the expected value of fighting. Compare it with the settlement.

The professional framing adds three adjustments. First, cost recovery: rules on who pays legal costs differ. In many Commonwealth courts the losing party is usually ordered to pay part of the winner's costs, while courts in the United States generally leave each side to pay its own, with exceptions. Verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Second, time value: money paid or received in two years is worth less than money today. Third, the hidden costs: management time, delay to the project, and the relationship.

Worked example one: a contractor's claim

All numbers are hypothetical. A contractor claims you owe 1,000,000 dollars for extra work. You believe you owe nothing. The contractor offers to settle today for 400,000 dollars. Your counsel estimates a 60 percent chance you win at trial in 2 years.

Step 1, legal costs. Your own legal costs to trial are 250,000 dollars, spread evenly, so assume they are paid on average at year 1.

Step 2, the win branch. You pay nothing on the claim, and counsel expects you to recover 40 percent of your legal costs: 0.40 times 250,000, which is 100,000 dollars received at year 2.

Step 3, the lose branch. You pay the 1,000,000 dollar claim plus pre-judgment interest, assumed at 100,000 dollars, plus a share of the contractor's costs, assumed at 100,000 dollars. Total 1,200,000 dollars paid at year 2.

Step 4, expected outcome at year 2. Win: plus 100,000 dollars times 0.60, which is plus 60,000 dollars. Lose: minus 1,200,000 dollars times 0.40, which is minus 480,000 dollars. Expected year-2 outcome: minus 420,000 dollars.

Step 5, discount at a hypothetical 8 percent. The year-2 amount: 420,000 divided by 1.08 squared, which is 420,000 divided by 1.1664, about 360,000 dollars. Your own legal costs at year 1: 250,000 divided by 1.08, about 231,000 dollars.

Step 6, total. Expected present cost of fighting: about 360,000 plus 231,000, which is about 591,000 dollars. Settlement: 400,000 dollars today. On these assumptions, settling is cheaper by about 191,000 dollars, before counting a single hour of your time.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example two: the breakeven probability

The weakest input is the 60 percent. Counsel's probability is a judgment, not a measurement. So ask a better question: how confident would you need to be for fighting to beat the settlement?

Let p be the probability you win. Using present values, the win branch is worth 100,000 divided by 1.1664, about 85,700 dollars. The lose branch is minus 1,200,000 divided by 1.1664, about minus 1,028,800 dollars. Legal costs are minus 231,000 dollars either way. The expected value of fighting is: p times 85,700, plus one minus p times minus 1,028,800, minus 231,000. Set that equal to minus 400,000, the settlement.

Work it through. p times 85,700 minus 1,028,800 plus p times 1,028,800 minus 231,000 equals minus 400,000. That gives p times 1,114,500 equals 1,259,800 minus 400,000, which is 859,800. So p equals 859,800 divided by 1,114,500, about 0.77. You would need roughly a 77 percent chance of winning just to break even with the settlement, before management time. If counsel says 60 percent, the decision is not close.

Where the probability comes from

Do not accept a single percentage without its reasoning. Ask counsel to break the case into the issues the other side must win. Suppose, hypothetically, the contractor must win two separate points: that the work was truly extra to the contract, and that it gave the notice the contract required in time. If counsel puts those at 50 percent and 80 percent, and treats them as independent, the contractor's chance of winning both is 0.50 times 0.80, which is 0.40, so your chance is 0.60. Now you can see which issue drives the number, test it against the documents, and focus your evidence there. A probability you can take apart is one you can improve.

The hidden costs

Add what the formula leaves out. If the dispute ties up a hypothetical 100 hours of your time and you value it at 300 dollars an hour, that is 30,000 dollars. If the contractor slows the remaining work and adds a hypothetical one month of delay to a project carrying 50,000 dollars a month in interest and overhead, that is another 50,000 dollars. And future bids from that contractor, and from others who hear about the dispute, may carry a premium. None of this means always settle. A settlement that rewards a weak claim teaches every contractor on your next job to file one. Sometimes the expected value says settle and the strategy says fight. Make that choice deliberately and write down why.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is fighting because you feel wronged rather than because the numbers or the strategy justify it. The control is to put every dispute above a set threshold through this tree in writing, with counsel's probability, the breakeven probability and the hidden costs, before you authorise anything beyond an initial response. Professional sign-off required: a litigation lawyer licensed in the jurisdiction, for the probability and the cost estimate.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner compares the settlement with the claim: 400,000 against 1,000,000, so settling feels like losing 400,000 for nothing. The real comparison is the settlement against the expected, time-adjusted cost of fighting. Seen that way, the 400,000 is often a discount.

Callback

In week 3 you studied loss aversion: people feel a loss more sharply than an equal gain. It drives bad litigation decisions. Paying a settlement feels like a certain loss, so people gamble on trial to avoid it, even when the expected cost of the gamble is higher. The tree is your defence against that bias.

Recap

Treat a dispute as an investment. Draw the tree, price each branch, discount for time and add the hidden costs. In the example, a 400,000 dollar settlement beat an expected present cost of fighting of about 591,000 dollars, and the breakeven probability of winning was about 77 percent. Next: LEX, The Room, on the meeting where the other side wants its own law and its own courts.
checklist: Draw the settle-or-fight tree for every dispute above your threshold
Get counsel's probability of success and full cost estimate in writing
Confirm the cost recovery rules in that jurisdiction
Discount every cash flow to today at a stated rate
Calculate the breakeven probability
Add management time, project delay and relationship costs
Write down the strategic reason if you fight against the numbers
Revisit the tree when new evidence or offers arrive
head: Field checklist
speak: A dispute is an investment. In my example, a contractor claims a million dollars and offers to settle for four hundred thousand. Counsel gives me a sixty percent chance of winning in two years. Fighting costs me two hundred fifty thousand in legal fees. If I win I recover some costs; if I lose I pay the claim plus interest plus part of their costs, about one point two million. Weighting each branch by its probability and discounting at eight percent, the expected present cost of fighting is about five hundred ninety thousand, against four hundred thousand to settle. Then I ask how sure I would need to be to make fighting worthwhile, and the answer is about seventy-seven percent. Then I add my own time, project delay and the relationship. Sometimes strategy still says fight, so I write down why. But the comparison is never settlement against claim; it is settlement against the expected cost of fighting.
terms: Expected value — the probability-weighted average of all possible outcomes of a decision.
Breakeven probability — the probability of winning at which fighting and settling have the same expected value.
Cost award — a court order requiring one party to pay some or all of the other party's legal costs, under rules that differ between jurisdictions.

hostile.q: You are settling a claim you told me was baseless. Doesn't that tell every contractor you can be squeezed?
hostile.a: I settled because the expected present cost of fighting was about 190,000 dollars higher than the settlement, and winning would have needed a confidence level counsel would not give. I did consider the signal it sends, which is why the settlement is confidential, includes a full release, and came with a change to our variation procedure so the same claim cannot arise on the next job. On a claim where the numbers favoured fighting, I would fight.

title: When they want their law and their court
summary: In a cross-border negotiation, the other side will often propose its own governing law and its own courts. The right response is neither to fold nor to fight for home advantage, but to ask what each side needs and propose a neutral, enforceable route. The scene shows what to say, what never to say, and when to stay quiet.
body:
When the other side proposes its own law and its own courts, they are rarely being aggressive. They are protecting themselves the same way you would. Your job is to find a governing law and a forum both sides can live with and that will actually produce an enforceable result.

Recall

Q. What was Rule 19?

A. No cross-border agreement is signed until it names its governing law, its forum and its escalation ladder, and counsel in each jurisdiction has confirmed the outcome can be enforced.

Q. In reverse engineering a deal, what do you do when your implied return looks too good?

A. Assume an input is wrong and go looking for it, usually the cost estimate or the rent assumption, before believing you have found a bargain.

Q. What is net present value used for when comparing two options?

A. It puts both options in today's dollars at the same required return, so you compare like with like rather than raw totals received at different times.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the governing law and forum conversation usually happens late, when everyone is tired and wants to sign. That is when people concede things they do not understand. Handled well, it takes ten minutes and protects the whole deal. Handled badly, it either collapses a good deal over a point of pride or buries a time bomb in the boilerplate.

The scene

A hypothetical joint venture to develop a mixed-use site. You are in the final negotiation meeting with your counterparty, a landowner from another country, and his lawyer. Your own counsel is with you. The commercial terms are agreed. The lawyer says: the agreement will be governed by our law, and any dispute goes to our courts. The land is here, after all.

The question behind the question

Before you answer, ask yourself what the lawyer is really protecting. Usually it is one of three things: familiarity, because he can advise confidently only on his own law; fear, because his client worries a foreign court will favour you; or enforcement, because a judgment from his own courts is easier to enforce against assets in his own country. Each of those needs a different answer, so find out which it is.

The lines to say

  • I understand why you would want that. Can you tell me what concerns you most about the alternatives?
  • We want the same thing: a dispute route that is quick, fair and produces a result either of us can actually enforce.
  • For questions about the land itself, the title, the registration and the permits, your law will apply whatever we write, and I am comfortable with that.
  • For the partnership obligations between us, I would like to look at a neutral option: arbitration under recognised rules, seated in a third place, with the agreement governed by a law both of our counsel know well.
  • Let our two counsel confirm in writing how an award would be enforced in each of our countries, and we will close on that basis.

Notice what the third line does. It concedes something true: property law usually follows the location of the land, whatever the contract says, so offering it costs little. Ask your counsel to confirm that for the specific jurisdiction. Conceding what is already true builds goodwill for the point that matters.

Say that out loud now.

The lines never to say

  • Your courts are too slow, or too unpredictable. Even if you believe it, you have just insulted his country in front of his client.
  • Our law is better. It is not your place to rank legal systems, and he will hear it as arrogance.
  • Fine, whatever is standard. There is no standard; there is only what you agree.
  • We will sort that out if anything goes wrong. That is exactly the sentence behind this week's Failure Forensics case, a composite joint venture that never named its court.

When to stay silent

After you ask what concerns him most, stop talking. Let him answer fully. The first concern people state is often not the real one, and silence draws out the second. And if he proposes something you do not understand, such as a particular court or arbitration rule, do not respond on the spot. Say: let me take that to counsel and come back to you tomorrow. Then do it.

And when he has finished, do not rush to fill the gap with a concession. A pause after the other side speaks often feels longer to you than it does to them. Let it sit for a few seconds, write a note, then respond to what was actually said rather than what you feared he would say. People who are comfortable with a short silence tend to concede less and learn more.

Worked example: what the forum choice costs

Hypothetical numbers. Suppose counsel estimates that a dispute in the landowner's courts would take about 4 years to final judgment at total legal cost to you of about 600,000 dollars, while arbitration in a neutral seat would take about 18 months at about 450,000 dollars, including arbitrators' fees. On a project where a dispute could freeze 10,000,000 dollars of equity that you value at a 12 percent annual opportunity cost, the time difference alone is worth about 12 percent times 10,000,000 times 2.5 years, which is about 3,000,000 dollars of opportunity cost. These are rough, but they show why forum is a commercial point and not only a legal one. Arbitration is not always faster or cheaper; that depends on the rules, the seat and the parties. Ask counsel for estimates for each option on your deal.

Holding your state

This is a moment where people feel cornered and get defensive. Notice your jaw and shoulders. Slow your speech. You are not defending national honour; you are solving a design problem with someone whose problem is the mirror of yours. If you feel your pulse rising, pause, take one slow breath out, and ask a question instead of making a statement. Questions lower the temperature in a room.

Cultural intelligence across Canada and Guyana

A monthly thread, and these are general norms, not rules about individuals. In Canadian business settings, people often expect a written agenda, direct statements of position, and decisions documented by email the same day. Disagreement is usually expressed openly but politely, and a delay in responding is often read as a lack of interest.

In Guyanese business settings, relationships and personal introductions often carry more weight early on, respect for seniority and title is commonly shown openly, and a decision may need time and conversations outside the meeting before it is final. Pressing for an answer in the room can read as disrespect. In both places, the safest habit is the same: ask how the other side prefers to work, and match it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is conceding governing law and forum late in a meeting to avoid conflict. The control is to decide your acceptable options with counsel before the meeting, including your walk-away point, and to treat governing law, forum and enforcement as commercial terms on the term sheet, not boilerplate for the end. Professional sign-off required: lawyers licensed in each jurisdiction.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner fights for home courts out of familiarity, wins the point, and then discovers that a judgment from his home court is hard to enforce against assets in the other country. Winning the clause is worthless if the result cannot be collected.

Callback

In week 6 you learned to handle hostile questions by acknowledging, bridging and answering. The governing law moment uses the same shape. Acknowledge the concern, bridge to the shared goal of a fair and enforceable route, and answer with a specific proposal.

Recap

When the other side wants its own law and courts, find out why: familiarity, fear or enforcement. Concede what is already true, such as the law of the land's location for title. Propose a neutral, enforceable route for the partnership obligations, and get enforcement confirmed by counsel on both sides. Stay silent after your question, and never insult their system. Next: Kema, Quiz and Recap, on how law works.
checklist: Decide acceptable governing law and forum options with counsel before the meeting
Put governing law and forum on the term sheet, not only in the final draft
Ask what concerns the other side most, then stay silent
Concede what is already true, such as the law governing the land itself
Propose a neutral and enforceable route for disputes between the parties
Never rank or criticise the other side's legal system
Take any unfamiliar proposal to counsel before answering
Ask how the other side prefers to work, and match it
head: Field checklist
speak: When the other side asks for its own law and its own courts, I do not fold and I do not fight for home advantage. First I ask what concerns them most, and then I stay quiet, because the first answer is rarely the real one. Usually it is familiarity, fear of a biased court, or enforcement. Then I concede what is already true: matters of title and registration follow the law of the place where the land sits. For the obligations between us as partners, I propose a neutral route, often arbitration in a third place under a law both counsel know, and I ask both counsel to confirm in writing how an award would be enforced in each country. I never say their courts are slow or our law is better. Forum is a commercial term with a real cost in time and money, so I settle it on the term sheet, not at midnight before signing.
terms: Arbitration — a private dispute process in which the parties agree to have one or more arbitrators decide their dispute, producing an award that can be enforced like a judgment, subject to the rules where enforcement is sought.
Seat of arbitration — the legal home of an arbitration, whose courts supervise the process and whose law governs the procedure.
Walk-away point — the least favourable terms you will accept before ending a negotiation, decided in advance.

hostile.q: The land is in our country. Why should a dispute about it be decided anywhere else?
hostile.a: Anything about the land itself, the title, registration and permits, will be governed by your law, and I am glad to say so in the agreement. What we are choosing is how disputes between the two of us as partners get decided. I want a route that is quick, that neither of us can see as favouring the other, and that produces a result both our countries' courts will enforce. Let our counsel compare options and confirm enforcement in writing, and I will accept the one that meets all three tests.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: How law works: quiz, Red Pen and boardroom
summary: Six questions to test the week on how law works: the legal stack, common and civil law, precedent, reading statutes, enforcement and settlement decisions. A Red Pen drill on a flawed file memo, and a two-minute boardroom explanation with a model answer.
body:
This week was about the machinery under every deal: where law comes from, who decides what it means, and what that is worth in money. If you can explain the legal stack, the two legal families and precedent in plain words, and price a dispute, you can hold your own with any lawyer.

Recall

Q. Why does slow enforcement push more equity into a deal?

A. Because a lender's expected loss on default grows with enforcement time, through unpaid interest, costs and a decaying asset, so it protects itself by lending a smaller share of cost.

Q. From last week's review of reverse engineering, what three things can you usually imply from public information about a competitor's deal?

A. The land price the deal can support, the rent it needs, and the return it is likely to earn, each with the uncertainty of the inputs you had to estimate.

Q. From week 11, what is the difference between net present value and internal rate of return?

A. Net present value is a dollar amount at a stated discount rate. Internal rate of return is the rate at which net present value is zero. One answers how much value; the other answers what rate.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is the foundation for the next six weeks: contracts, liability, tax and using professionals all sit on top of it. Test yourself honestly. If an answer below surprises you, go back to that day's lesson before moving on.

The six questions

Question 1. A zoning by-law and a valid provincial statute conflict on a parking requirement. Which usually prevails, and what do you do before relying on that?

Answer: The higher layer, the valid statute, usually prevails over the by-law where it properly covers the point. Before relying on it, get counsel's written view on the exact wording and any cases that interpret it, and keep the higher cost in the base case until you have it.

Question 2. What is the core difference between a common-law and a civil-law system?

Answer: Common-law systems build much of their law through judges' decisions and precedent, with statutes layered on top. Civil-law systems build private law around a comprehensive written code that judges apply. Most of Canada and Guyana are common-law; Quebec is civil-law.

Question 3. A trial decision from another province supports your position. Does it bind the court that will hear your case?

Answer: No. Only decisions of higher courts in the same hierarchy bind. A decision from another province or country is persuasive at most, and only the reasoning necessary to the decision carries weight.

Question 4. In what order should you read a statute?

Answer: Definitions, purpose, the operative rule, exceptions, transitional provisions, then the regulations made under it and the cases that interpret it, after confirming the version in force from an official source.

Question 5. What was Rule 19?

Answer: No cross-border agreement is signed until it names its governing law, its forum and its escalation ladder, and counsel in each jurisdiction has confirmed the outcome can be enforced.

Question 6. A contractor offers to settle a 1,000,000 dollar claim for 400,000 dollars. What do you compare the 400,000 against?

Answer: Against the expected, time-discounted cost of fighting, including your legal costs, cost recovery rules, the probability-weighted outcome, and hidden costs like delay and management time. Not against the size of the claim. Then check the breakeven probability.

Say that out loud now.

Red Pen drill

A hypothetical memo to file. Read it once and find the defects before you read the answers.

Memo. Joint venture with an overseas landowner. One: we do not need a governing law clause, because the land is overseas and that country's law automatically governs everything in the agreement. Two: a 2021 trial decision from another province is directly on point and will bind any court that hears a dispute. Three: the city's parking by-law requires 1.0 space per unit and overrides the regional statute because it is more specific. Four: I checked the act online this morning, so the text is current. Five: counsel says our case against the contractor is strong, so we should litigate rather than settle. Six: settling at 400,000 dollars on a 1,000,000 dollar claim means we lose 400,000 dollars for nothing.

The defects. One: the law of the land's location usually governs title and registration, not necessarily every partnership obligation; the agreement still needs a governing law clause and a forum. Two: a trial decision from another province binds nobody outside its own hierarchy; it is persuasive at most. Three: a lower layer does not override a valid higher one simply by being more specific; that needs counsel's analysis of the actual wording. Four: an online text may be an unofficial or out-of-date consolidation, and amendments may not be in force; check the official version on the relevant date. Five: a strong case is a probability, not a decision; run the settle-or-fight tree and the breakeven probability. Six: the settlement must be compared with the expected cost of fighting, not with zero.

Boardroom drill

Explain how law works to a hypothetical investor in two minutes. Then compare with the model answer.

Model answer: Every deal we do is a bundle of legal rights, so I start by knowing where the rules come from. The constitution sets who can make law; statutes, regulations and by-laws sit beneath it, each valid only within the power given by the layer above; courts interpret all of them; and our contracts write private law for the parties. Canada and Guyana are both common-law systems at their core, so court decisions matter as much as the statute, and only decisions from higher courts in the same hierarchy bind. Quebec is the exception in Canada, with a civil code. In every new jurisdiction, I get written answers to three questions before committing money: which law governs, which court or tribunal decides, and how long enforcement takes. That last one drives what lenders will advance, and therefore how much equity we need. Every agreement we sign names its governing law, its forum and an escalation ladder. And when a dispute arises, I price it: probability, cost, time and the breakeven, against the settlement on the table.

Now do it for real. Set a timer for two minutes and say your version out loud, without notes. If you run over, you are explaining too much law and not enough decision; cut the detail and keep the three questions you ask in every jurisdiction. If you stumble on precedent, use one sentence: only higher courts in the same hierarchy bind. Then compare your version with the model and note the one point you left out. That gap is what you review next week.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is false confidence: having learned the shape of the system, assuming you can now reach legal conclusions yourself. The control is to use what you learned to ask sharper questions and judge the answers, while every real decision still rests on advice from a lawyer licensed in the jurisdiction. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer licensed in the jurisdiction.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner memorises case names. The names matter much less than the method: identify the layer, find the definitions, check what binds, confirm the version in force, and price the outcome.

Callback

In week 5 you learned the pyramid principle: bottom line first, then the supporting points. The boardroom answer above follows it. It opens with why law matters to the deal, gives three supporting points, and ends with what you actually do. Use that shape whenever you explain law to people who are not lawyers.

Recap

Law is a stack, two families organise most of the world's systems, precedent binds only from above, statutes are read in order and in context, slow enforcement costs equity, and disputes are priced like investments. Rule 19 protects every cross-border agreement. Next: LEX, First Principles, on how a contract is formed.

head: The six questions
speak: This week was the machinery under every deal. Law is a stack: the constitution, then statutes, then regulations and by-laws, each valid only within the power given from above, with courts interpreting all of it and contracts writing private law for the parties. Most of Canada and Guyana use common law, where judges' decisions matter as much as the statute; Quebec uses a civil code. Only decisions from higher courts in the same hierarchy bind; everything else persuades. I read statutes in order, starting with the definitions, and I confirm the version in force. Lenders price enforcement time, so a slow legal system costs me equity. Rule 19: no cross-border agreement is signed until it names its governing law, its forum and its escalation ladder, with enforcement confirmed by counsel on both sides. And I price every dispute against the settlement on the table, not against the claim.
terms: Binding precedent — a decision of a higher court in the same hierarchy that a lower court must follow.
Persuasive authority — a decision or source a court may consider but is not required to follow, such as a decision from another jurisdiction.
Escalation ladder — a contract's staged dispute process, typically notice, negotiation, mediation, then a final decision by a named court or tribunal.

hostile.q: You keep saying you would get local counsel's view. At what point do you actually know enough to make a decision yourself?
hostile.a: I make the commercial decision; counsel tells me the legal facts it rests on. I know enough to frame the questions precisely, read the statute and the key cases myself, and spot when an answer is vague or inconsistent. What I will not do is replace a licensed opinion with my own reading on a point that moves money. The decision is mine; the legal conclusion is theirs, in writing.
